text: Lesson 77 covered the DataFrame API. This lesson covers the two ways Snowpark logic becomes a reusable, callable object inside Snowflake — a user-defined function you call inside a query, and a stored procedure you call, or schedule, to run a whole piece of logic.

The decorator form turns a Python function into a callable SQL function in one step. Temporary is the default — scoped to your session, gone when it ends, which is right for development. A permanent UDF needs is_permanent equals True and a stage_location, because Snowflake has to upload the Python file somewhere durable so it still exists in the next session, and the next person's session. Once registered, you call it exactly like any built-in SQL function.
A Snowpark Python Worksheet doesn't have to stay a one-off script. Click Deploy on the toolbar, and Snowsight offers to turn the worksheet itself into a stored procedure.

Name the procedure, and deploy it. Nothing about the underlying Snowpark logic changes — you're just giving Snowflake a durable, callable version of the exact code you already tested in the worksheet.
Once it's deployed, you'll find it under Data, Databases, Procedures, listed with its language as Python — a real object other code, and other people, can call.

This is exactly what Chapter 8's Tasks are built to schedule. Instead of a Task running one hardcoded SQL statement, it can call a Snowpark stored procedure that reads a Stream's changed rows, transforms them with DataFrame logic, writes the result, and logs what happened — all as one schedulable unit.
Next lesson covers what Snowflake built on top of Secure Data Sharing: a way to share application logic itself, not just raw tables — and even sell it on the Snowflake Marketplace.
